items.q: At its core, how does a large language model produce an answer?
options: It predicts the next token (word-piece) from patterns it learned, one piece at a time
It looks the answer up in a built-in database of facts
It runs your code and reports what happened
It searches the live internet for every question by default

explain.right: An LLM is a next-token predictor; it generates text one likely piece at a time from learned patterns.
explain.wrong: It has no fact database and no default internet access; those require tools. It isn't executing code either.

items.q: Why might an LLM not know about something that happened very recently?
options: Its knowledge comes from training done at a point in time (a cutoff); newer info must be given to it or fetched by a tool
Recent events are too small to matter to it
It forgets things over time like a person
It only knows things its current user has told it

explain.right: Training happens once at a point in time, so the base model has a knowledge cutoff; current facts come via context or tools.
explain.wrong: It doesn't 'forget'; its weights are frozen after training. It knows far more than just what the user said.

items.q: An LLM confidently gives you a function name that turns out not to exist. This is best described as:
options: A hallucination — a plausible-sounding but incorrect prediction
Proof the model is broken and unusable

explain.right: It predicts plausible text even when it doesn't truly 'know', producing confident-but-wrong output called a hallucination.
explain.wrong: It isn't a machine fault or intentional lying, and it doesn't make the model useless — it means you verify consequential output.

items.q: In one or two sentences: why should you double-check code an LLM writes, even when it sounds confident?
rubric: Mentions it predicts plausible text, not verified truth
Mentions confidence in tone does not equal correctness / it can hallucinate
Implies verifying by running it or checking against the spec

explain.right: Good answers note that fluent confidence isn't correctness, so you verify by running it / checking the spec.
explain.wrong: A weak answer just says 'because computers make mistakes' without the prediction/confidence idea.
